messages.subject: Model fit great but loadings terrible - can this be?
parts:
Dear all,

I have a question regarding the ambiguous information I get with lavaan from the modell fit on the one hand and the loading of the variables on the other hand: I'm trying to fit a measurement model with multimodal biological data from the same brain roi (functional, resting state, structural, MRS data) who are already standardized (sex/age partialled out with linear regression, multivariate normal but have about 20 missings). According to the model fit the model seems pretty great (too good actually) but when looking at the loadings (no significant loadings onto the lv at all) the model is everything but good (see below). Do you have any suggestions how this can be? What have I missed here? A modindices() check also didnt show anything.
The parallel analysis (from exploratory factor analysis) has shown that the eigenvalues are extremely low (see attached). Could it have something to do with that? I'd be very thankful for any ideas!

messages.author: 0325c6a976085eab
messages.subject: Re: Model fit great but loadings terrible - can this be?
parts:
This is not ambiguous.  As factor loadings decrease, fit (as measured by chi-square) improves.

Imagine if all your loadings were zero, your chi-square (and RMSEA) would also be zero. 

Look at your null model - that does not have a significant chi-square - in other words, if all of your loadings were zero, your model would still fit. 

Jeremy

messages.subject: Re: Model fit great but loadings terrible - can this be?
parts:
Dear Jeremy,

first of all, thanks so much for your answer!!!  Unfortunately I only partially understand what you mean: On the one hand, you say that if the loadings decrease the chi-square improves but then you say if my loadings are extremely decreased (zero) the chi-square would be zero (?) So should the chi-square improve or decrease with decreasing loadings (I thought chi-square should decrease).

Best,
Maxi

Am Mittwoch, 28. Januar 2015 01:23:10 UTC+1 schrieb Jeremy Miles:
This is not ambiguous.  As factor loadings decrease, fit (as measured by chi-square) improves.

Imagine if all your loadings were zero, your chi-square (and RMSEA) would also be zero. 

Look at your null model - that does not have a significant chi-square - in other words, if all of your loadings were zero, your model would still fit. 

Jeremy

Sorry, I'll try to be clearer. 

A lower chi-square means a better fitting model fit.So (usually) a lower chi-square = improved chi-square.  

Jeremy

messages.author: 6a75f6f91a59c568
messages.subject: Re: Model fit great but loadings terrible - can this be?
parts:
In my opinion, sample size was too small for your data.

In general, structural equation modeling requires over 200 samples, but your data wasn't satisfied.

I don't know what you were measured, but I can recommend to trying the common factor analysis; do not try principle component analysis. The common factor analysis can be calculated model fit indices with TLI and RMSEA by a psych package.

--
Seongho Bae
